name: Hember Avu
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Read Pick 2020 (PhD, UH Manoa): stress data 'minimal or nonexistent' for most Northern Adelbert languages; only Z'graggen 1971/1980 wordlists cover Hember Avu

new_statements.quote: Of the vowels, e and o represent ɛ and ɔ; there is no phonemic distinction between close and open varieties and hence no need to use the special symbols. Stress is free and may occur on any syllable, even finals. The only uncommon consonant cluster is mkj in senamkja, "slow."
new_statements.citation: Capell, Arthur. 1952. Languages of the Bogia District, New Guinea (continued). Oceania 22(3): 178-207. Section 13 'Vanembere' [= Musar / Hember Avu]. DOI 10.1002/j.1834-4461.1952.tb00559.x
new_statements.locator: p. 195, sec. 13 'Vanembere', paragraph following the phoneme table (PDF page 31 of the archive.org issue scan)
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is not tied to a fixed position: it may fall on any syllable of the word, including the final one; Capell marks it lexically in his examples and wordlist (initial in 'mande 'man', 'emi 'hair', 'ndayngumo 'eye'; non-initial in mande'mayngem 'woman', e'kwa:k 'head', himbe'ravu 'mouth', o'kokona 'some').
new_statements.exceptions: None; no minimal pairs and no conditioning factors are given, so 'free' here means positionally unfixed rather than demonstrably contrastive.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (citation forms in a c. 200-item survey wordlist plus a few sentences); 1949 survey data from speakers met at Bogia hospital and mission/area schools, not in the villages; Capell's part-1 introduction adds that none of the Bogia languages is tonal.
new_statements.identity_note: The statement is Capell's (1952) sketch of 'Vanembere' (his transcription βa'nembərɛ), collected in 1949 from speakers met at Bogia. Z'graggen 1971 (PL C-19, p. 52) first equated Capell's Vanembere with Wanambre (Mokati/Tinami area), but Z'graggen 1980 (PL D-31, p. vii) corrected this: Capell's Vanembere wordlist 'is practically identical with the present writer's Musar word list and should thus be regarded as representing the Musar language and not the Wanambre language', and Pick 2020 (p. 111 fn. 39) independently states 'Capell's (1952) description of what is clearly Hember Avu is also labeled Vanembere.' So the source describes Musar = Hember Avu, musa1265 [mmi] (also called Amben, Aregerek). Capell's wordlist forms (e.g. 'mande 'man', amben 'hand') match Z'graggen's F11 Musar column. No dialect is specified; SIL's 2000 orthography drafts distinguish 'Upper Amben' and 'Lower Amben (Musar)' varieties.

sources.note: p. 195 (PDF p. 31), after the Vanembere phoneme table: 'Stress is free and may occur on any syllable, even finals.' Examples and the wordlist carry stress marks ('mbateta 'jaw', o'kokona 'some', 'mande 'man', mande'mayngem 'woman', e'kwa:k 'head', himbe'ravu 'mouth'). Vanembere = Musar/Hember Avu per Z'graggen 1980: vii and Pick 2020: 111 fn. 39. Page image checked visually.

sources.citation: Pick, Andrew. 2020. A reconstruction of Proto-Northern Adelbert phonology and lexicon. PhD dissertation, University of Hawai'i at Manoa. 485 pp.
sources.note: Sec. 1.5.1 'Stress' (pp. 31-32): stress described only for Mauwake, Pamosu, Usan; 'the available data on stress in most languages are minimal or nonexistent'. Sec. 3.4 Hember Avu (pp. 118-124; author's 2016 wordlist, Z'graggen recordings, SIL orthography drafts): phoneme inventory, verb morphology, nasal spreading, e-rounding; nothing on stress. Fn. 39 (p. 111): 'Capell's (1952) description of what is clearly Hember Avu is also labeled Vanembere.'

sources.citation: Z'graggen, J. A. 1980. A comparative word list of the Northern Adelbert Range languages, Madang Province, Papua New Guinea. Pacific Linguistics D-31. Canberra: ANU. Musar = F11.
sources.note: p. vii: 'Capell's (1952: 203ff) Vanembere word list is practically identical with the present writer's Musar word list and should thus be regarded as representing the Musar language and not the Wanambre language.' Sec. 7 p. ix: transcription 'semi-phonemic'; Musar fluctuations -k~0, l~r, y~j, h~f. Musar forms carry vowel-length marks but no stress marks; nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Z'graggen, J. A. 1975. The Madang-Adelbert Range Sub-Phylum. In Wurm (ed.), New Guinea Area Languages vol. 1, PL C-38, 569-612.
sources.note: F11 Musar population 684; comparative pronoun/lexical rows; nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Z'graggen, J. A. 1971. Classificatory and typological studies in languages of the Madang District. Pacific Linguistics C-19. Canberra: ANU. Musar = language 29 (Mr), Mawamuan Family.
sources.note: Sec. 2.22.23.12 Musar (p. 52): villages, 'Previously unrecorded', named after Musar Mountain; Mawamuan typology (pp. 52-53): segmental notes (l/r contrastive in Musar, prenasalized voiced stops, negation postposed); sec. 2.22.8: 'None of the languages appears to be tonal.' No statement on stress. Here Capell's Vanembere is still equated with Wanambre (corrected in 1980).
